metadata.title: Why are there differences across German states in student achievement and cognitive ability?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study aggregates state-level means across multiple external achievement and cognitive-ability sources (PISA, PIRLS, IQB, and a German armed forces intelligence test) and then computes correlations, regressions, and path models on N=16 German federal states. The methodology does not describe the use of complex survey sampling weights (e.g., student-level design weights) from the underlying ILSA microdata; instead, it uses published state means and standardized/averaged scale scores. Because the analysis is conducted at the state level (ecological aggregation) rather than on individual student records, standard ILSA student sampling weights are not applicable in the way they would be for microdata PV-based estimation. The paper also standardizes and averages across years and dimensions before combining study means, and it applies robustness checks via partial correlations (removing west–east and city–rural differences) and outlier exclusions (e.g., Bremen, Brandenburg).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are state-level aggregated means (e.g., PISA/PIRLS/IQB state averages and percentile-threshold groups) and other macro indicators, not student-level cognitive achievement scores generated via ILSA plausible values. Plausible Values are therefore not applicable because the analysis does not estimate PV-based achievement for individual students. Missing-data handling is not reported at the level of the underlying ILSA microdata; instead, the paper discusses issues in reported migration-background information and uses averaging/standardization across published state results, but it does not provide a formal missing-data procedure for the aggregated dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The unit of analysis is the 16 German federal states (N=16). The study constructs state-level achievement/cognitive-ability indicators by extracting published state means from: PISA 2000/2003/2006 (reading, mathematics, science; plus problem solving in 2003), PIRLS 2001/2006 (fourth-grade reading), and IQB studies 2009/2011/2012/2015/2016 (curriculum-related dimensions at fourth and ninth grades), plus the Bundeswehr intelligence test 1998 (young men without conscientious objection). For each study, the authors average across dimensions within a study (and across years after common standardization) to form overall student achievement/cognitive ability means; they also use 05% and 95% percentile-threshold groups and Gymnasium vs. other tracks, and they compute natives vs. migrants means based on reported migration background (noting that an unknown migration-background group is likely weak and may bias migrant/native differences). Foreign-language dimensions are excluded from the averaging process in IQB. Robustness checks include partial correlations removing west–east and city–rural differences and outlier sensitivity analyses (e.g., removing Bremen/Brandenburg for some correlations).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000/2003/2006 (15-year-olds) Reading/Mathematics/Science (state means, N=16 German states)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlations: with conservative educational policies mean r = .90 (cognitive ability mean) and r = .93 (student mean); politics (votes burgher-civic-conservative-right) rSA = +.78; education policy (path/regression) β ≈ .45 (education policy effect) and β ≈ .41 (policy effect) in regression predicting student achievement studies mean; path model: education policy β = .63 and education quantity β = .29; within education indicators: traditional instruction (PISA) r = .55 (cognitive ability mean) and r = .63 (student mean).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000/2003/2006 state-mean the study leveraged conservative educational policies, migration background share, state government political orientation, Klafki proximity, and student discipline to explain state differences in student achievement mean, finding that more conservative and achievement-based education policies and lower migration-background shares are associated with higher achievement. This indicates that tightening achievement standards (e.g., central exams, discipline, and traditional instruction) may align with higher state-level achievement, though the evidence is correlational and based on a small N of 16 states.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2001/2006 (fourth graders) Reading (state means, N=16 German states)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlations reported across education indicators: central exit examinations (1995) r = .76 (cognitive ability mean) and r = .79 (student mean); discipline r = .71 (cognitive ability mean) and r = .77 (student mean); tracking at young age r = .35 (student mean at 05% threshold) and r = .36 (cognitive ability mean). The paper reports overall homogeneity of the combined achievement/ability pattern across studies with Cronbach-α = .93 for the overall student achievement score (PISA, PIRLS, IQB).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2001/2006 reading state-mean the study leveraged conservative education policy indicators, migration background share, state government political orientation, discipline, and central examinations to explain state differences in student achievement mean, finding that discipline and centralized examinations are positively associated with achievement while more progressive/less achievement-oriented policy orientations are negatively associated. This indicates that reading achievement at the state level may co-vary with broader system-level governance choices (exam centralization and classroom management), though causal claims cannot be established from aggregated correlations.

main_findings.dataset_used: IQB 2009/2011/2012/2015/2016 (fourth and ninth graders) Reading/German/Foreign languages/Mathematics/Science (state means, N=16 German states)
main_findings.target_variable: Cognitive ability mean (state-level, combined across IQB dimensions excluding foreign languages)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlations: politics (votes burgher-civic-conservative-right) rCA = +.82 and governments rCA = +.90; conservative educational policies mean r = .90 (cognitive ability mean); Klafki proximity r = −.83; achievement structure r = .75; discipline r = .71; comprehensive school rate r = −.74; Gymnasium rate r = −.45; high-school rate (Abitur) r = −.75. Path model: political orientation of state government → education policy β = .87; education policy → cognitive competence (student achievement mean) β = .63; education quantity → cognitive competence β = .29.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using IQB 2009/2011/2012/2015/2016 state-mean cognitive ability the study leveraged state government political orientation, conservative education policy, migration background share, achievement structure, and Klafki proximity to predict cognitive ability mean, finding that more conservative and achievement-oriented education policies and lower migration-background shares are associated with higher cognitive ability. This indicates that system-level policy orientation may be linked to cognitive outcomes at the state level, but the analysis is ecological (16 states) and therefore cannot confirm individual-level causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This Heliyon study examines differences across the 16 German federal states in student achievement and cognitive ability by aggregating published state-level results from PISA (2000/2003/2006), PIRLS (2001/2006), IQB (2009/2011/2012/2015/2016), and a Bundeswehr intelligence test (1998). The authors compute correlations, regressions, and cross-sectional/longitudinal path models (including cross-lagged effects) on state-level means rather than training ML models on microdata. The combined achievement/ability pattern is highly homogeneous (Cronbach-α = .93), and the strongest associations are with political orientation and education policy: votes/governments for burgher-civic-conservative-right parties correlate positively with cognitive ability (e.g., rCA ≈ +.82 to +.90) and student achievement (rSA ≈ +.78 to +.88), while Klafki proximity is strongly negative (r ≈ −.83). The paper reports standardized path coefficients (e.g., education policy β ≈ .63; education quantity β ≈ .29) and discusses robustness via partial correlations and outlier removal. Limitations include the small N of states, ecological inference risk, and the absence of PV-based estimation and formal missing-data handling for underlying microdata.
